forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Luton procurement exemptions reach 680 in 2025/26, up from 321 in 2023/24, mostly children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Requests to bypass Luton Council's normal buying rules (exemptions to standing orders) rose to 680 in 2025/26, from 321 in 2023/24 and 566 the year before, the Audit & Governance Committee is told in its annual procurement report. The council approved 471 of them, with £41.8m in approved value.

Children, Families & Education accounted for 311 of the requests, 46% of the total. Its requests were worth £40.6m, 57% by value, and the council approved 244 of them (78%) and £21.4m of the value (53%). The report attributes the increase largely to residential care and foster care placements, out-of-borough school places for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), and home-to-school transport. Rejections also rose, to 209 from 119 in 2023/24. About 44% were for administrative errors and 17% for missing conflict-of-interest declarations.

The council has set up a Passenger Transport Services Framework, a compliant route for buying home-to-school transport, which accounted for about £2.6m of exemption value in 2025/26. The paper says this is expected to "significantly reduce" future requests in that area. Members are asked to acknowledge that the council's processes, commissioning arrangements and procurement policies need further review for residential care, foster care and out-of-borough school placements.

The committee also has the first-quarter budget monitoring (the in-year check of spending against budget). Adult social care is forecasting a £1.7m overspend from demand and complexity, and the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with SEND, a £2.8m overspend even after an approved £880k transfer from the Schools Block. The corporate risks paper says the council balanced its 2026/27 budget without using reserves, helped by a 5% council tax rise and the government funding settlement, after a significant 2025/26 deficit that it did not size. It is pursuing a deficit recovery plan over two years.

On internal audit, of 349 recommendations followed up, 76% were fully implemented, 20% were in progress and 4% not yet started.

news_drafts.headline: Luton complaints handling falls short of 80% target despite quarterly improvement
news_drafts.lead: Luton's complaints performance reached 62.4% in-service-level agreement (in-SLA) in the year to March 2026, falling 17.6 percentage points short of the 80% target the council set for the first time in January. The council showed quarterly progress, rising from 60.8% in the first quarter to 65.5% in the fourth, and ombudsman compensation claims dropped 69% to £4,750. However, Children, Family & Education — the highest-risk area — saw complaints surge 54% to 216 while performance remained flat at 34.3% in-SLA, leaving cases unresolved at an average of 52.9 days against an 80% target. The council has committed to a dedicated recovery plan with weekly leadership review and targets of 60% in-SLA by the end of the second quarter and 75% by year-end, conditional on training completion and new platform implementation.

news_drafts.headline: Luton Council uses emergency reserves to balance budget as spending pressures mount
news_drafts.lead: Luton Council's budget forecast for 2026/27 balances only after deploying £1.764m of its contingency—money set aside to cover unexpected costs—to offset underlying spending pressures of £2.533m. The council faces demand-led pressures across adult social care and schools special needs support. Adult social care forecasts a £1.7m overspend despite additional government funding to address chronic underfunding, driven by demographic growth and rising care costs. The High Needs Block—the part of school funding for children with special needs and disabilities—forecasts a £2.83m overspend after a surge in requests for assessments following national education reforms. Planned savings are slipping into the next financial year. The council is also reviewing its capital spending programme—money for long-term assets like buildings and roads—due to concerns about the cost of borrowing.

findings.headline: Council housing condition survey shows 96.31% of stock rated decent as of June 2026, with planned works to reach 100% by December 2028
findings.detail: Conditions survey completed. Works sequenced across kitchens, bathrooms, roof replacements, rewires, and boilers throughout council housing stock. Programme tracks against target of 98% by March 2027 and 100% by December 2028.
findings.matters: Asset management and housing standard compliance; capital programme execution tracking
findings.figures: 96.31% decent (reported to MHCLG June 2026); target 98% March 2027, 100% December 2028

findings.paper_title: 7. Appendix B - Corporate Performance Q1 26-7 - PowerPoint
findings.headline: Anti-social behaviour incidents reported at 986 in Q1 2026-7, above target, though council notes increased reporting of incidents is likely a driver
findings.detail: Monthly ASB incidents 986 in Q1 26/7 vs 870 in Q1 25/6, trending above seasonal adjustment. Council explicitly encouraging reporting and noting that increased numbers likely reflect increased reporting of genuine issues rather than increase in actual incidents. Plan to understand drivers and respond in next quarter.
findings.matters: Service demand and potential resource cost indicator; community safety perception signal; actual trend unclear
findings.figures: 986 monthly incidents Q1 2026-7 (vs 870 Q1 2025-6); target 3130 annual
findings.quote: We are encouraging residents to report anti-social behaviour which is likely leading to an increase in the numbers recorded.

findings.paper_title: 7. Appendix B - Corporate Performance Q1 26-7 - PowerPoint
findings.headline: Residents agreeing that Luton is a town where people get on well fell from 77% to 73%, while those believing they can influence local decisions fell from 41% to 36%
findings.detail: Two-measure decline in civic cohesion and sense of agency; cohesion target is 83% by 2028, influence target 45% by 2028. Council delivering We Are Luton campaign (120,000 social media interactions, 30 groups involved) and resident engagement events but measures still moving away from targets.
findings.matters: Community cohesion and civic engagement declining despite council investment; signals community perception and trust concerns
findings.figures: Cohesion: 77% (2024) to 73% (2025); Influence: 41% (2024) to 36% (2025); targets 83% and 45% respectively by 2028
findings.quote: Residents who tend to agree or defintely agree that Luton is a town where people from different backgrounds get on well together 77% (2024) 73% (2025)

findings.paper_title: 7. Appendix B - Corporate Performance Q1 26-7 - PowerPoint
findings.headline: Resident satisfaction with Luton as a place to live remained at 50%, unchanged, against target of 57% by March 2027
findings.detail: Annual measure only; no progress visible yet despite initiatives including 97 place activation events, 69 social events, and 1200 residents engaged in feedback. Council exploring options for collecting data more frequently to track impact sooner.
findings.matters: Community perception and council service quality baseline; failure to progress despite investment indicates either measurement lag or initiative ineffectiveness
findings.figures: 50% satisfaction (unchanged from baseline); target 57% March 2027, 65% by December 2028
findings.quote: This is an annual measure from the residents survey. As data is only currently collected annually, we have yet to see the impact of current initiatives on this measure.
